# Week 78 Appendix: The Week the Clock Held Its Breath

*Fatal ICE shootings, a war resumed without authorization, and a primetime bid to relitigate 2020 nearly offset each other to a standstill.*

![Header image](image_wide_week78_appendix.png)

This week combined an active foreign war, an ICE fatality crisis, a direct assault on press freedom, and an unprecedented presidential campaign against election legitimacy—all compressed into seven days. Trump resumed strikes on Iran without congressional authorization, subpoenaed New York Times reporters over Air Force One security coverage, and delivered a primetime address recycling debunked 2020 election fraud claims while threatening broadcast licenses of networks that declined to air it. Simultaneously, DHS officials threatened state election officials with criminal prosecution for refusing voter-roll demands, and Trump ousted independent election commissioners—actions widely read by Democrats as groundwork for contesting the midterms. ICE's mass-enforcement surge produced multiple fatal shootings of non-target civilians, prompting a policy reversal within 24 hours after Trump personally overrode a brief operational pause. Judicial pushback (the Williams ruling voiding the IRS settlement) and a Senate blockade of the NDAA offered rare institutional resistance, but were overshadowed by executive assertions of unchecked power, including firing a judicially appointed U.S. attorney within an hour of his swearing-in.

Power and Authority

1. Trump refused to sign a bipartisan housing bill to pressure the Senate on voting restrictions (2026-07-11): The president let a housing bill become law without his signature while using his leverage to demand passage of a separate voter-restriction measure, mixing unrelated policy areas for political gain.

2. Trump notified Congress of resumed strikes on Iran, restarting the War Powers Act clock (2026-07-11): The administration claimed a fresh 60-day window for military action against Iran without new congressional authorization, testing constitutional limits on presidential war powers.

3. Trump held a secret Camp David meeting with select House Republicans to craft a reconciliation funding package (2026-07-11) *[single source]*: Selective invitations, confiscated phones, and exclusion of moderate lawmakers show an attempt to control legislative deliberation outside normal process.

4. Trump posted threats of massive missile strikes against Iran on social media (2026-07-11): Public threats of large-scale destruction against a foreign nation, issued outside formal channels, escalated tensions and bypassed deliberative national-security process.

5. Trump ordered airstrikes on Iran following closure of the Strait of Hormuz (2026-07-12): Unilateral military strikes expanded an active conflict without new congressional authorization, reinforcing executive dominance over war-making decisions.

6. President continued national emergency declarations on transnational crime and hostage-taking (2026-07-13): Renewal of standing emergency declarations extends executive authority to impose sanctions and restrictions without fresh legislative review.

7. Trump tied renewal of a foreign surveillance law to passage of a voting-restriction bill (2026-07-13) *[single source]*: Conditioning national security legislation on a partisan election measure subordinated intelligence oversight to electoral advantage.

8. Trump announced then reversed a naval blockade and toll scheme for the Strait of Hormuz (2026-07-13): A declared blockade of a major international waterway, a potential act of war, was abandoned within a day after diplomatic pushback, reflecting erratic unilateral military and trade decision-making.

9. Trump declared a national energy emergency and shrank two Utah national monuments by roughly 90 percent (2026-07-14) *[single source]*: Executive proclamations stripped federal protection from millions of acres of public land, bypassing legislative and administrative review to favor extractive industry.

10. Atlanta Mayor Andre Dickens stated intent to exclude unhoused people from the city ahead of the World Cup (2026-07-12) *[single source]*: A public official's stated goal to remove a vulnerable population from public spaces set the stage for enforcement actions raising equal-access concerns.

11. Trump constructed a helipad on the White House South Lawn without congressional or regulatory review (2026-07-16): A major infrastructure project proceeded on federal grounds by bypassing statutory zoning, environmental, and legislative oversight, funded partly by a defense contractor with business before the administration.

12. Trump overruled his own administration's suspension of ICE vehicle stops and directed agents to resume them (2026-07-15): The president reversed a brief safety pause following two fatal shootings, prioritizing enforcement volume over accountability measures within a day of their announcement.

13. Trump ordered DHS to purge noncitizens from state voter rolls and demanded Congress pass a voting-restriction bill (2026-07-17) *[single source]*: The president directed use of a voter-screening tool federal courts have repeatedly blocked and pressured lawmakers to pass restrictive voting legislation ahead of the midterms.

14. Trump removed three members of an independent federal election administration commission (2026-07-13): Ousting independent election commissioners ahead of midterms raised concerns about executive interference in nonpartisan election administration.

15. Trump fired a judicially appointed U.S. attorney within an hour of his swearing-in (2026-07-17): Immediate removal of a judge-panel-appointed federal prosecutor demonstrated presidential assertion of control over prosecutorial appointments meant to be judicially insulated.
